title: Creditors’ Rights and Strategic Default: Evidence from India
venue: The Journal of Law and Economics
abstract: I examine whether stronger creditors’ rights prevent strategic default. Borrowers who cross either of two thresholds are exempt from a creditor-rights law in India. Using a loan-day-level data set, I find that loan performance is better when the law applies and that outperformance increases after a further rise in creditors’ rights. To discern the strategic motive, I use an unprecedented invalidation of the Indian currency whereby holders of high-value currency were forced to declare their cash holdings to banks. Defaulters exempt from the law showed a greater tendency to repay their loans after invalidation.

summary.oneLiner: In India, stronger creditor rights are linked to better loan performance, and the evidence suggests they curb strategic default.
summary.overview: This paper asks whether stronger creditor rights stop borrowers from strategically defaulting, meaning they can pay but choose not to. Borrowers just above or below two thresholds are exempt from a creditor-rights law, which lets the author compare loan performance with and without the law. Loans perform better when the law applies, and the gap grows after creditor rights are strengthened further. To isolate the strategic motive, the author uses an invalidation of high-value Indian currency that forced holders to declare their cash to banks; borrowers exempt from the law were more likely to repay afterwards.
summary.question: Do stronger creditors' rights prevent strategic default?
summary.method: The author compares borrowers who fall on either side of two thresholds that determine whether they are exempt from a creditor-rights law. To identify the strategic motive, the author uses the invalidation of high-value Indian currency as a setting that separates defaulters by exemption status. The abstract does not name the specific statistical technique.
summary.data: A loan-day-level data set from India. The abstract does not state the sample size, lenders, or time period.
findings: Loan performance is better when the creditor-rights law applies to the borrower.
The outperformance increases after a further rise in creditors' rights.
Defaulters exempt from the law showed a greater tendency to repay their loans after the currency invalidation, which the author uses to discern the strategic motive.
summary.whyItMatters: The paper's evidence that stronger creditor rights are associated with better loan performance and less strategic default bears on how lenders and policymakers weigh creditor protection. The abstract does not spell out specific managerial or policy recommendations.
